pages.wrong_reason: Inverted direction. Factoring hardness is NOT known to imply RSA hardness. The known reduction runs the other way: factoring N recovers phi(N) and hence the secret exponent d, so an efficient factoring algorithm breaks RSA, i.e. RSA hardness implies factoring hardness. Whether breaking RSA (computing e-th roots mod N) is as hard as factoring is a long-standing open problem, with evidence against certain reduction types (Boneh-Venkatesan, Eurocrypt 1998, rule out algebraic/straight-line reductions for small e; DLO24 gives an equivalence only in the generic ring model with preprocessing, recorded at red-rsa-to-fac-dlo24). RSA78 proves no implication from factoring to RSA; it introduces the trapdoor permutation whose only known attack route is factoring. The correct edge is RSA => FAC (folklore: factoring breaks RSA).
flags: Matches suspected-errors entry for content/Assumptions/factoring.md:29 (recorded there under id red-factoring-to-ra-rsa78; this page's frontmatter id is red-fac-to-rsa-rsa78 — same claim, spelled differently).

The wiki records only the generic-ring-model equivalence (content/Reductions/rsa-to-fac-dlo24.md, model: other). A plain standard-model folklore edge RSA => FAC ('factoring N breaks RSA') does not yet exist and is the correct replacement for this page's content.
The migrated bullet's parenthetical 'factoring may be harder than RSA' is itself backwards for the same reason (RSA may be easier than factoring is the open direction's usual phrasing).

sources.ref_file_title: Jer16 - Integer factoring and modular square roots
sources.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences 82(2), pp. 380–394
sources.note: DOI 10.1016/j.jcss.2015.08.001 (verified via ACM DL and ScienceDirect). Not in cryptobib; use inline bibtex. Shows factoring is reducible in randomized polynomial time to a PPA problem and to WEAKPIGEON in PPP; derandomizable under GRH.

pages.class_justification: A containment between complexity classes is proved unconditionally by any argument; per repo convention (see e.g. bpp-to-pspace), proven inclusions take class: free.
pages.statement: The search problem underlying [[factoring|FAC]] — given a positive integer $N$, output its prime factorization — lies in [[total-function-np|TFNP]]: every positive integer has a prime factorization, and a candidate factorization is verified in polynomial time by multiplying the factors and testing each for primality — folklore.
pages.sketch: Totality is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic; the polynomial-time verifier checks $\prod_i p_i^{e_i} = N$ and the primality of each $p_i$.
pages.improvements_text: - Factoring reduces in randomized polynomial time to a problem in PPA and to $\text{WeakPigeon} \in$ PPP, placing it in these TFNP subclasses; both reductions derandomize under the generalized Riemann hypothesis — [[Jer16 - Integer factoring and modular square roots|Jer16]]
flags: The second sentence of the migrated quote ('Recent work has used TFNP subclass hardness (especially PPAD) as a basis for constructing cryptographic primitives') carries a suspected direction error tracked in .reductions/suspected-errors.json (total-function-np.md:37, affecting red-ph-to-cpg) — it does not affect this containment and should not be reintroduced here.

sources.ref_file_title: BBS86 - A Simple Unpredictable Pseudo-Random Number Generator
sources.authors: Lenore Blum, Manuel Blum, Michael Shub
sources.note: cryptobib_key: BluBluShu86. DOI 10.1137/0215025. Introduces the x^2 mod N generator over Blum integers; proves unpredictability under the quadratic residuosity assumption. Earlier version: Crypto 1982 (C:BluBluShu82).

sources.ref_file_title: VV84 - Efficient and Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generation
sources.authors: Umesh V. Vazirani, Vijay V. Vazirani
sources.note: cryptobib_key: C:VazVaz84. FOCS 1984 extended abstract: DOI 10.1109/SFCS.1984.715948. Proves the x^2 mod N generator secure assuming only that factoring Blum integers is hard, replacing BBS86's quadratic residuosity assumption; also extracts O(log log N) bits per iteration.

pages.class_justification: The generator is one fixed algorithm; the hypothesis enters only as the hard instance $N$ (with its promised factor structure). The security proof is one fixed reduction that runs any PRG distinguisher solely as an oracle: Yao's hybrid argument converts it into a predictor for the parity of a principal square root, which factors $N$. Construction and reduction are both fixed and oracle-respecting — the fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: If [[factoring#factoring-with-known-factor-structure|factoring Blum integers]] — $N = pq$ with $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ — is hard, then a [[pseudorandom-generator|PRG]] exists: the Blum–Blum–Shub generator iterates squaring modulo $N$ and outputs the parity of each state — [[BBS86 - A Simple Unpredictable Pseudo-Random Number Generator|BBS86]]. BBS86 prove unpredictability under the quadratic residuosity assumption; [[VV84 - Efficient and Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generation|VV84]] prove it assuming only hardness of factoring Blum integers.
pages.sketch: Sample $x \getsr \ZZ_N^*$, set $x_0 = x^2 \bmod N$ and $x_{i+1} = x_i^2 \bmod N$, and output $\mathrm{lsb}(x_1), \ldots, \mathrm{lsb}(x_m)$. A distinguisher yields a next-bit predictor, i.e. a predictor for the parity of the principal square root of a random quadratic residue; such a predictor extracts square roots modulo $N$, and two distinct square roots of the same residue factor $N$.
pages.improvements_text: - Security assuming only hardness of factoring Blum integers (BBS86 assumed quadratic residuosity), and $O(\log \log N)$ output bits per squaring — [[VV84 - Efficient and Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generation|VV84]]
notes_to_keep: factoring-blum-integers has no page; the hypothesis is addressed via the anchor [[factoring#factoring-with-known-factor-structure]].

pages.wrong_reason: The hypothesis 'falsifiable assumption' is a meta-category of assumptions, not a well-defined object, so the hyperedge is untypeable as stated (the migration notes concede this). The underlying bullet is also imprecise about the source: Gro16 proves knowledge soundness of the Groth16 SNARK unconditionally in the generic (bilinear) group model — an idealized-model lower-bound-style argument, not a reduction from a falsifiable assumption — and the frontmatter's model: algebraic-group misattributes it; the AGM analysis of Groth16 (under the q-DLOG assumption, which is falsifiable) is due to FKL18, not Gro16. Correctly typed replacements: a GGM-model edge sourced to Gro16, and a q-dlog => snark edge with model: algebraic-group sourced to FKL18 (both papers have wiki reference pages).
flags: The same migrated bullet also spawned content/Barriers/no-falsifiable-assumption-to-snark-gro16.md; the barrier half (no black-box reduction of SNARG soundness to falsifiable assumptions in the standard model) is the Gentry–Wichs result (GW11, STOC 2011) and should be sourced there, not to Gro16.

If a positive edge is wanted, the concrete hypotheses are: generic-group model (Gro16) or q-DLOG in the AGM (FKL18) — two records, matching the migration note that the bullet is disjunctive over models.

pages.wrong_reason: Degenerate hyperedge, malformed beyond repair as typed: the title asserts 'hash-based signatures + hash-based signatures => DS' — the hypothesis set is the conclusion's own subclass listed twice — and the frontmatter hypotheses (few-time-signature, xmss) are concrete scheme artifacts with no pages, not model objects. The substantive result — stateless many-time hash-based signatures from hash functions — is the SPHINCS construction (Bernstein, Hopwood, Hülsing, Lange, Niederhagen, Papachristodoulou, Schneider, Schwabe, Wilcox-O'Hearn, Eurocrypt 2015) and SPHINCS+ (Bernstein, Hülsing, Kölbl, Niederhagen, Rijneveld, Schwabe, CCS 2019), and belongs on a hash-function => DS edge.

sources.note: The identification protocol and the signature scheme.

sources.ref_file_title: FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems
sources.note: The transform: replace the verifier's challenge by a hash of the commitment and the message.

sources.ref_file_title: PS96 - Security Proofs for Signature Schemes
sources.note: cryptobib_key: EC:PoiSte96. First EUF-CMA proof for Schnorr signatures in the ROM under DLOG, via the forking lemma. Journal version: Security Arguments for Digital Signatures and Blind Signatures, J. Cryptology 13(3), 2000 (JC:PoiSte00).

pages.model_justification: The challenge is a hash value modeled as a programmable random oracle; the PS96 EUF-CMA proof rewinds the forger and reprograms the oracle, and no standard-model proof from DLOG is known.
pages.statement: Applying the [[fiat-shamir-heuristic|Fiat–Shamir transform]] to the Schnorr identification protocol — a three-message public-coin proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm — yields the Schnorr signature scheme, a [[digital-signature|DS]]: the signer computes the challenge as $c = H(R \| m)$, so a signature is a non-interactive protocol transcript — [[Sch91 - Efficient signature generation by smart cards|Sch91]], [[FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems|FS86]]. The scheme is $\eufcma$-secure in the random-oracle model under the [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] assumption — [[PS96 - Security Proofs for Signature Schemes|PS96]].
pages.sketch: The reduction runs the forger, then rewinds it to the forking hash query and reprograms the random oracle; two accepting transcripts $(R, c, s)$ and $(R, c', s')$ with $c \neq c'$ yield the secret key as $x = (s - s')/(c - c')$ (forking lemma).
pages.security_loss: Non-tight: the forking-lemma reduction turns a forger with success probability $\varepsilon$ making $q_H$ random-oracle queries into a DLOG solver with success roughly $\varepsilon^2/q_H$ (PS96).
flags: Structural: hypothesis 'fiat-shamir' is a transform, not an object, and 'schnorr-identification-protocol' has no page — the edge does not fit the object/hyperedge model cleanly; class left unstated because the RTV taxonomy does not apply to a transform-plus-concrete-protocol hyperedge and no source assigns a class (the PS96 reduction is black-box in the forger, via rewinding, but programs the random oracle).
Near-duplicate of red-fiat-shamir-and-schnorr-signatures-to-schnorr-signatures-sch91 (same hypotheses; conclusion ds vs schnorr-signature) — consider merging into one page.

sources.ref_file_title: FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems
sources.note: Introduced the transform; the NIZK-in-ROM formulation is the standard adaptation, universally cited to this paper.

pages.model_justification: Soundness of the compiled argument and zero knowledge (via oracle programming) are both proved with the hash modeled as a programmable random oracle; in the standard model the transform can fail (see the GK03 barrier pages).
pages.statement: Applying the [[fiat-shamir-heuristic|Fiat–Shamir transform]] to a constant-round public-coin interactive proof that is [[zero-knowledge-proof#honest-verifier-zk-hvzk|honest-verifier zero-knowledge]] and has negligible soundness error yields a [[non-interactive-zero-knowledge|NIZK]] argument in the random-oracle model: each verifier challenge is replaced by a hash of the statement and the transcript so far — [[FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems|FS86]].
pages.sketch: Honest-verifier simulation suffices because the compiled challenges are exactly the uniform challenges an honest verifier would send; the simulator runs the HVZK simulator and programs the random oracle so its transcripts verify.
flags: The migrated sentence names no conclusion; the migration inferred NIZK with low confidence. The statement records the standard true result, but the load-bearing qualifiers (public-coin, constant rounds, negligible soundness error) are absent from the source text and were added — without them the claim is false (HVZK alone gives no soundness, and FS on super-constant-round proofs loses soundness).
Hypothesis 'honest-verifier-zero-knowledge' is a property/section anchor, not an object page; 'fiat-shamir' is a transform, not an object.
Near-duplicates: red-zkp-to-nizk-fs86 and red-rom-and-zkp-to-nizk-fs86 record the same transform — consider consolidating.
Class left unstated: no source classifies the transform in RTV terms.

sources.ref_file_title: Seu12 - On the Exact Security of Schnorr-Type Signatures in the Random Oracle Model
sources.note: cryptobib_key: EC:Seurin12. Meta-reduction showing the forking lemma's q_H security loss is essentially optimal for algebraic reductions from DLOG.

pages.model_justification: The challenge is a hash value modeled as a programmable random oracle; the PS96 security proof rewinds the forger and reprograms the oracle.
pages.statement: The Schnorr signature scheme is the [[fiat-shamir-heuristic|Fiat–Shamir transform]] applied to the Schnorr identification protocol: for a generator $g$ of a group of prime order $q$ and key pair $(\sk, \pk) = (x, g^x)$, signing $m$ samples $r \getsr \ZZ_q$ and sets $R = g^r$, $c = H(R \| m)$, $s = r + cx$; the signature $(R, s)$ is an accepting transcript with hash-derived challenge, verified by $g^s = R \cdot \pk^c$ — [[Sch91 - Efficient signature generation by smart cards|Sch91]], [[FS86 - How to Prove Yourself Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems|FS86]]. The scheme is $\eufcma$-secure in the random-oracle model under the [[discrete-logarithm|DLOG]] assumption — [[PS96 - Security Proofs for Signature Schemes|PS96]].
pages.sketch: The reduction runs the forger, rewinds it to the forking hash query, and reprograms the random oracle; two accepting transcripts $(R, c, s)$ and $(R, c', s')$ with $c \neq c'$ yield $x = (s - s')/(c - c')$ (forking lemma).
pages.security_loss: Non-tight: the forking-lemma reduction turns a forger with success probability $\varepsilon$ making $q_H$ random-oracle queries into a DLOG solver with success roughly $\varepsilon^2/q_H$ (PS96).
pages.improvements_text:
- $\eufcma$ security in the ROM under DLOG, via the forking lemma — [[PS96 - Security Proofs for Signature Schemes|PS96]]
- The forking lemma's $q_H$ loss is essentially optimal: a meta-reduction rules out tighter algebraic reductions from DLOG — [[Seu12 - On the Exact Security of Schnorr-Type Signatures in the Random Oracle Model|Seu12]]
notes_to_keep: The [[Sch91 - Efficient signature generation by smart cards]] reference page says the identification protocol 'is honest-verifier zero-knowledge under the discrete logarithm assumption'; Schnorr's sigma protocol is perfect HVZK unconditionally — DLOG underlies soundness/impersonation resistance, not HVZK.
The EdDSA/Ed25519 lineage claim in the migrated text is uncited and is not carried by this edge.
flags: Near-duplicate of red-fiat-shamir-and-schnorr-signatures-to-ds (same hypotheses; conclusion schnorr-signature vs ds) — consider merging; if both are kept, this page is the specific instance and that one the generalization.
Conclusion 'schnorr-signature' has no object page (anchor digital-signature#schnorr-signatures is used); hypothesis 'fiat-shamir' is a transform and 'schnorr-identification-protocol' has no page.
The migrated quote wrote $r \getsr \ZZ_p$ and $s = r + cx \bmod p$ with $p$ doubling as group order; the statement normalizes to prime order $q$.
Class left unstated: the RTV taxonomy does not apply to a transform-plus-concrete-protocol hyperedge and no source assigns a class.

pages.wrong_reason: FRI alone does not imply a SNARK, and the migrated sentence carries a flagged terminology error: FRI is an IOP of proximity (a low-degree test for closeness to Reed–Solomon codewords), not a polynomial commitment scheme — a polynomial commitment (and then a SNARK) is built from FRI plus Merkle hashing, and the STARK construction additionally needs arithmetization (AIR/ALI) and the BCS compilation in the ROM. As a single-hypothesis hyperedge 'fri => snark' the claim is false: the hash function and arithmetization hypotheses are missing. The correctly typed edge already exists as content/Reductions/arithmetization-and-fri-fast-reed-solomon-iop-of-proximity-to-snark-bbhr18.md (with hash-function-to-snark-bbhr18.md and hash-function-to-pcs-bbhr18.md covering the hash hypothesis), sourced to BBHR18, which has a wiki reference page.
flags: Matches the suspected-errors entry for content/Primitives/succinct-argument.md:77 (affectsEdges: red-fri-to-sa) — FRI mislabeled as a polynomial commitment scheme.

The FRI protocol's own citation is BBHR18a ('Fast Reed-Solomon Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity', ICALP 2018), distinct from the wiki's existing BBHR18 STARK paper; if a FRI object page is ever created, that reference stub is still missing.

sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
sources.note: Defines FSS as the generalization of DPF (introduced in GI14) to arbitrary function classes; the specialization is definitional.

sources.ref_file_title: BGI16 - Function Secret Sharing Improvements and Extensions
sources.authors: Elette Boyle, Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
sources.note: Refined FSS definitions and improved concrete DPF/FSS constructions.

pages.class_justification: The construction is the identity: a DPF is the FSS scheme itself with its function class restricted to point functions, invoked as-is; any DPF adversary is verbatim an FSS adversary for the same class. Both the construction and the security reduction are fixed and use their objects only as oracles — trivially the fully-black-box shape.
pages.statement: A [[distributed-point-function|DPF]] is [[distributed-point-function#function-secret-sharing-fss|function secret sharing]] for the class of point functions: an FSS scheme for any function class $\calF$ containing all point functions $f_{\alpha,\beta}$ — where $f_{\alpha,\beta}(\alpha) = \beta$ and $f_{\alpha,\beta}(x) = 0$ for $x \neq \alpha$ — is in particular a DPF — [[BGI15 - Function Secret Sharing|BGI15]].
pages.sketch: Run the FSS key generation on the point function $f_{\alpha,\beta}$; correctness (the keys' outputs add to $f_{\alpha,\beta}(x)$) and key privacy restrict verbatim to the subclass.
pages.improvements_text: - Refined FSS definitions and improved concrete DPF/FSS constructions — [[BGI16 - Function Secret Sharing Improvements and Extensions|BGI16]]
notes_to_keep: 'function-secret-sharing' has no page or slug; FSS is defined only inside the DPF page's Variations section despite being the more general object.
flags: Direction is correctly oriented (FSS => DPF, specialization); the surface phrasing 'DPFs are a special case of FSS' invites inversion, as the migration noted.
DPFs themselves predate FSS — introduced in GI14 (reference page exists); BGI15 is the right original for this specialization edge since it defines FSS.
